techniques.name: Reframe nerves as excitement
techniques.summary: Instead of trying to calm down before a high-stakes moment, relabel the racing heart as excitement. Arousal stays high but points towards opportunity rather than threat.
techniques.how_to_apply: Just before the meeting or turn, tell yourself (silently or aloud) that you are excited and name what you are excited to get across. Do not try to suppress the arousal.
techniques.drill: Before each of the next five high-stakes meetings, say 'I'm excited about X' once. The coach compares first-five-turn pitch and rate with meetings where you did not.

techniques.name: Long-exhale reset
techniques.summary: A few breaths with an exhale longer than the inhale lower physiological arousal within a minute or two. It is the fastest legal sedative before a hard conversation.
techniques.how_to_apply: Two to five cycles: a full inhale through the nose, a short top-up inhale, then a slow, long exhale through the mouth. Do it in the minute before speaking or while someone else is talking.
techniques.drill: Daily for two weeks: five minutes of exhale-focused breathing, then use two cycles before every meeting you chair. Track first-turn pitch against baseline.

sources.where: Balban et al. 2023, cyclic sighing arm
breath as the base of presence

techniques.name: Settle your pitch in the first turns
techniques.summary: The opening minutes set your rank in a group: people whose pitch climbs early tend to be ranked lower, those who settle lower and steadier gain influence. The aim is your own relaxed level, not an artificially deep one.
techniques.how_to_apply: Make your first one or two contributions short and on firm ground, at your relaxed conversational pitch. Breathe out before the first word.
techniques.drill: For four weeks, plan a short, easy first line for each group meeting. The coach charts first-five-turn pitch drift week by week.

sources.where: Cheng et al. 2016, early pitch change and emergent rank
Ko et al. 2015, power and voice

techniques.name: Let the end of your turn breathe
techniques.summary: Confident speakers do not rush to fill the silence after their point or tack on extra clauses. A clean stop followed by a beat of silence signals that you are not afraid of the response.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you have made your point, stop, hold a one to two second silence, and let others respond. Resist adding 'so, yeah' or a second version.
techniques.drill: For a week, end every substantive turn in meetings with a full stop and silence. The coach counts turn-final trailers before and after.

sources.where: Charisma Myth: pausing and not rushing

techniques.name: Slow down for the sentence that matters
techniques.summary: You do not need to slow down everything; slowing and pausing around the key claim, number or decision makes it register and remember better while the rest can run at normal speed.
techniques.how_to_apply: Mark the one sentence per turn that carries the point. Slow it, pause before the key word, and pause after it.
techniques.drill: Read a three-paragraph update aloud, slowing only the headline sentence. Record it; the coach compares rate on the headline vs. the rest.

sources.where: MacGregor et al. 2010, pauses before words aid memory
Jobs vs. Zuckerberg rate and phrasing
pace as one of five vocal elements

techniques.name: Same voice after the jab
techniques.summary: When a comment stings, hold your volume, pitch and pace exactly where they were. A visible jump in any of them is the clearest audible sign that someone got to you.
techniques.how_to_apply: On the turn after a provocation, consciously match your previous loudness and rate, start with a short neutral sentence, then answer.
techniques.drill: With a colleague, rehearse five provocative challenges. Answer each at baseline volume and pace; the coach reads loudness and rate on each reply.

sources.where: Ko et al. 2015: vocal cues of power

techniques.name: Let minor errors pass
techniques.summary: Correcting every small inaccuracy or slight makes you look anxious about status. Restraint means choosing which points are worth contesting.
techniques.how_to_apply: When someone misstates something minor, ask yourself whether it changes the decision. If not, let it go or note it after the meeting.
techniques.drill: For one week, write down every correction you were tempted to make in meetings and whether it mattered. Make only the ones that did.

sources.where: dominance vs. prestige routes to influence

techniques.name: Do not laugh off your own point
techniques.summary: Nervous laughter after your own serious statement undercuts it. Laughter that only you produce, with no one joining, usually signals discomfort rather than ease.
techniques.how_to_apply: After making a serious point, hold a neutral face and voice. Save laughter for when something is actually funny.
techniques.drill: The coach lists every Tom-only laugh for two weeks with the line before it. Pick the pattern (e.g. after bad news) and drop it for the following two weeks.

sources.where: Bitterly et al. 2017: failed humour lowers status

techniques.name: Own it in one breath, then fix
techniques.summary: When something you own went wrong, a short, plain admission followed straight away by the fix reads as strength. Long explanations read as defensiveness.
techniques.how_to_apply: One sentence of ownership with 'I', one sentence of what you are doing about it. No preamble, no blame, no third sentence of justification.
techniques.drill: Think of a recent mistake. Write and say the two-sentence version until it comes out in under 15 seconds.

sources.where: Owens & Hekman 2012: admitting mistakes as humble leadership
Tenney et al.: calibration and credibility

techniques.name: A deliberate beat before hard answers
techniques.summary: A short, visible pause before answering a difficult question can read as thought rather than panic, especially if a crisp answer follows. But long gaps before agreeing to a request can sound reluctant.
techniques.how_to_apply: On a hard or important question, pause about one to two seconds, then open with a direct first sentence. On simple requests you are happy to grant, answer promptly.
techniques.drill: In a mock Q&A, take a full breath before each answer and open with yes, no or a number. The coach checks gaps and first words.

techniques.name: Land the full stop
techniques.summary: Let pitch fall at the end of a statement so it sounds finished and owned. A rise at the end of a recommendation turns it into a request for approval and invites interruption.
techniques.how_to_apply: On recommendations, decisions and introductions, let the last stressed word drop to a low, settled pitch and hold a beat of silence after it.
techniques.drill: Read ten recommendation sentences aloud, landing each with a falling pitch and one-beat pause. The coach checks final_rise_st on each.

sources.where: Charisma Myth: lowering intonation at sentence ends

techniques.name: Speak from your natural pitch, not a forced low one
techniques.summary: Lower voices are associated with leadership perceptions, but later work found pitch predicts electability rather than ability, and forcing the voice down causes strain and creak. The coachable goal is your relaxed, breath-supported pitch that does not climb under pressure.
techniques.how_to_apply: Find your relaxed pitch (e.g. say 'mm-hmm' as if agreeing with a friend) and return to it before key turns. Never try to sound deeper than that.
techniques.drill: Each morning for a week, hum and speak a sentence at relaxed pitch; before key meetings repeat once. The coach tracks pitch stability, not level.

sources.where: Ko et al. 2015: power raised pitch slightly
Love: finding the natural speaking voice

techniques.name: Breathe before the sentence, not mid-sentence
techniques.summary: Taking a low, full breath before you start a sentence gives the voice support to the end. Running out of breath leads to rushing, trailing off and creaky endings.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before a key sentence, breathe low (belly expands, shoulders still), then speak the whole thought on that breath. Shorten sentences if you run out.
techniques.drill: Read a paragraph aloud taking one low breath per sentence. Repeat daily for a week; listen for sentence endings staying full.

sources.where: Set Your Voice Free: breathing chapter

techniques.name: Stress the operative word
techniques.summary: In each important sentence, one or two words carry the meaning. Giving them a pitch peak and slight loudness bump makes the point audible without any extra words.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before speaking, pick the operative word (often the number, the contrast or the verb) and lift pitch and volume a touch on it.
techniques.drill: Mark one operative word per sentence in a short script and read it twice: flat, then stressed. The coach compares pitch_sd_st.

sources.where: Toastmasters vocal variety: where to place emphasis
animated voice as a charismatic tactic

techniques.name: Widen your pitch range when persuading
techniques.summary: Speakers rated as more charismatic use more pitch movement. Monotone delivery in a pitch or recommendation reads as low energy or low belief.
techniques.how_to_apply: In persuasive turns, let your voice move more than in routine updates: higher on the new or exciting idea, lower on the conclusion.
techniques.drill: Read a paragraph twice, 'to a friend' and 'to a board'; keep the board version varied but slower. Compare pitch_range_st.

techniques.name: Contrast in loudness, not more loudness
techniques.summary: Authority comes from varying volume to mark what matters, not from being loud throughout. Greater loudness variability is linked to perceived dominance and power.
techniques.how_to_apply: Keep a comfortable base volume and add a small lift on key words; occasionally drop volume to draw people in on a crucial point.
techniques.drill: Deliver a two-minute update with one deliberate quiet moment and two lifted key words. The coach checks loudness_sd_db.

sources.where: Ko et al. 2015: loudness variability in high-power speakers

techniques.name: Pause before the key word
techniques.summary: A short silent pause just before an important word or number makes listeners attend to it and remember it better.
techniques.how_to_apply: Place a half to one second silence right before the number, name or decision you want remembered.
techniques.drill: Before any number in your next five meetings, pause one beat. The coach checks pause placement before numerals in the transcript.

sources.where: Conrad et al. 2013: brief frequent pauses

techniques.name: Pause after the point to let it land
techniques.summary: After a key point, silence gives listeners time to absorb it and signals confidence. Rushing on makes the point feel disposable.
techniques.how_to_apply: After a headline, a striking fact or a decision, stop for one to two seconds before moving on.
techniques.drill: Record a three-minute presentation with a two-second silence after each of your three main points; listen back for impact.

techniques.name: Swap fillers for silence
techniques.summary: Filled pauses ('um', 'uh', 'you know') make listeners think you know less, and are the strongest single cue to perceived uncertainty. A silent pause does the same planning job without the cost.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you feel a filler coming, close your mouth and pause instead. Focus on fillers just before your main claim first.
techniques.drill: Record a two-minute impromptu answer daily for a week, replacing every 'um' with silence. The coach tracks fillers_per_100w.

techniques.name: Finish the sentence you started
techniques.summary: False starts and abandoned sentences are part of the 'powerless' style that lowers credibility. Finishing one complete sentence beats starting three.
techniques.how_to_apply: If you lose the thread, finish the current sentence simply, pause, then start the next thought cleanly.
techniques.drill: Answer five unexpected questions with a rule: first sentence under 12 words and complete. The coach counts restarts.

sources.where: Get to the Point: complete points

techniques.name: Late-night radio voice to calm things down
techniques.summary: A slower, lower, softer, downward-inflected voice calms a tense exchange better than telling people to calm down. Voss presents it as his de-escalation register.
techniques.how_to_apply: When tension rises, drop your pace and volume a notch and let sentences end downward. Keep it warm, not patronising.
techniques.drill: Rehearse three tense scenarios with a colleague using the calm register; the coach compares rate and loudness against your normal challenge replies.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference; MasterClass on tone

techniques.name: Warm, light default register
techniques.summary: For most work conversation, a relaxed, positive tone (smiling in the voice) makes people more cooperative and open than a flat or assertive tone. The assertive register is best kept for rare moments.
techniques.how_to_apply: Default to an easy, upbeat tone; let a smile into the voice on greetings and requests. Reserve the clipped, assertive tone for a real line in the sand.
techniques.drill: In the first minute of each 1:1 this week, open with a light, warm line. The coach notes laughter and the other person's first-turn length.

techniques.name: Warm up the voice before big meetings
techniques.summary: Singers and actors warm up; speakers rarely do. A few minutes of humming, lip trills and sirens makes the first words of the meeting sound like the tenth.
techniques.how_to_apply: Five minutes before: hum on a comfortable note, do lip trills sliding up and down, then say your opening line aloud twice.
techniques.drill: Do a five-minute warm-up before the next three presentations; compare your first-turn pitch and loudness with meetings where you did not.

techniques.name: Vary pace with meaning
techniques.summary: Pace is a tool: slower for weight, risk and decisions; a little quicker for context and momentum. Studies disagree on whether faster or slower is better overall, which is a reason to vary, not to fix one speed.
techniques.how_to_apply: Speed up slightly through background, slow down for the conclusion and any number, and avoid speeding up when challenged.
techniques.drill: Record a two-minute update in three segments (context, finding, recommendation) at three deliberate speeds. The coach plots rate by segment.

sources.where: Smith et al. 1975 rate; Tusing & Dillard 2000

techniques.name: Short phrases, short sentences
techniques.summary: Shorter phrases between pauses and shorter sentences are easier to follow, easier to stress and leave fewer chances to stumble. The more charismatic speaker in Niebuhr's comparison used shorter phrases.
techniques.how_to_apply: Break long thoughts into short sentences of one idea each. One clause, breathe, next clause.
techniques.drill: Take one long sentence from last week's transcript and rewrite it as three. Say both versions aloud and record.

techniques.name: Watch the creak at phrase ends
techniques.summary: Vocal fry (a creaky, low rattle at the end of phrases) often comes from running out of breath. One study found it penalised, but critics say the speakers were imitating fry unnaturally.
techniques.how_to_apply: Take a breath before you run out, keep a little air at sentence ends, and avoid pushing pitch below your comfortable floor.
techniques.drill: Read a paragraph aloud recording only sentence endings; repeat with a breath before each sentence and compare.

sources.where: Anderson et al. 2014 and Liberman critique

techniques.name: Project to the back of the room (or the far microphone)
techniques.summary: Presence needs to be heard. Quiet, swallowed speech loses authority in rooms and on calls, and makes people ask you to repeat, which costs momentum.
techniques.how_to_apply: Aim your voice at the furthest person (or into the mic at a steady distance). Keep energy to the end of each sentence.
techniques.drill: In an empty room, speak a paragraph to the far wall without shouting; then do it to a phone recording from across the room and check every word is clear.

techniques.name: Bottom line up front
techniques.summary: Put the conclusion, recommendation or answer in the first sentence, then the reasons, then detail. A busy listener can stop at any point and still have the point.
techniques.how_to_apply: Start substantive turns with 'My recommendation is', 'The answer is' or 'In short'. Context comes after, and only if needed.
techniques.drill: Before each update this week, write one sentence starting 'I recommend' or 'The answer is' and say it first. The coach checks claim position.

sources.where: Pyramid Principle: start with the answer
Simply Said: lead with the message

techniques.name: The 'I believe that' test
techniques.summary: A topic is a subject area; a point is a claim someone could disagree with. If your opening cannot follow 'I believe that...', you have a topic, not a point.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before speaking, finish the sentence 'I believe that...' and use the completion as your opening line.
techniques.drill: Take the agenda of your next meeting and turn each item into an 'I believe that' sentence before you go in.

sources.where: Get to the Point: point vs. topic, 'I believe that' test

techniques.name: Point, reason, example, point
techniques.summary: A simple four-beat structure for a contribution: state the point, give the main reason, give one concrete example, restate the point. It keeps impromptu contributions short and complete.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use PREP for any contribution longer than a sentence or two; aim for under a minute.
techniques.drill: Answer five practice questions with PREP aloud, each under 45 seconds. The coach checks the four beats.

techniques.name: Situation, complication, question, answer
techniques.summary: For topics that need context, a short opener names the situation everyone agrees on, the complication that changed it, the question this raises, and then your answer. It keeps context brief and purposeful.
techniques.how_to_apply: Spend one sentence each on situation, complication and implied question, then give your answer and support.
techniques.drill: Rewrite your next status update as four lines (S, C, Q, A) and say it in under 40 seconds.

techniques.name: Announce the number of points
techniques.summary: Telling listeners how many points are coming ('three reasons') gives them a map, signals preparation and makes it easier to hold the floor until you finish.
techniques.how_to_apply: Say the number before the list, then label each one ('first', 'second'). Keep it to two or three.
techniques.drill: In every substantive turn this week, announce a count before listing. The coach checks announced vs. delivered counts.

techniques.name: Distinct reasons that cover the case
techniques.summary: Supporting points should not overlap and together should cover what the listener needs. Overlapping reasons sound like padding; gaps invite the obvious challenge.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before a key meeting, list your reasons and check: does any repeat another? Is there an obvious category missing (cost, risk, people, time)?
techniques.drill: Take last week's main recommendation and sort its reasons into non-overlapping groups. Cut the duplicates.

techniques.name: What? So what? Now what?
techniques.summary: A three-part structure for impromptu contributions: what is happening, why it matters, what we should do next. Useful when asked for a view without warning.
techniques.how_to_apply: When called on, organise your reply into the three beats, one or two sentences each.
techniques.drill: Ask a colleague for five random workplace questions; answer each with What/So what/Now what in under 45 seconds.

sources.where: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: What-So What-Now What

techniques.name: Problem, solution, benefit
techniques.summary: For proposals: name the problem, propose the solution, state the benefit. It moves a listener from concern to action in three beats.
techniques.how_to_apply: Frame proposals as a problem the listener recognises, your fix, and what they get.
techniques.drill: Draft your next proposal in three sentences using the pattern and rehearse it aloud.

techniques.name: Make abstractions concrete
techniques.summary: Concrete language (specific numbers, names, objects, examples) is easier to understand, more memorable and makes listeners feel heard. Abstract corporate language feels evasive.
techniques.how_to_apply: For every abstract claim, add one concrete anchor: a number, a person, a place or a picture.
techniques.drill: The coach picks three abstract sentences from last week's transcript; rewrite each with a number, a person or an image.

sources.where: Bezos Blueprint: plain language and analogies

techniques.name: Plain words and no weasel words
techniques.summary: Simple words and short sentences make you sound clearer and more confident. Vague softeners ('sort of', 'kind of', 'basically') and passive voice blur ownership.
techniques.how_to_apply: Choose the plain word, use active voice ('we missed the date', not 'the date was missed'), and remove vague softeners.
techniques.drill: Edit a page of your own notes to an easy reading level, then present from the edited version.

sources.where: Bezos Blueprint: plain writing, weasel words, active voice

techniques.name: Close by restating the headline
techniques.summary: End a contribution or presentation by returning to the main point in a single sentence. Listeners remember beginnings and ends; a trailing ending wastes the strongest position.
techniques.how_to_apply: Finish substantive turns with 'So, ...' plus your headline, then stop.
techniques.drill: For each turn longer than 30 seconds this week, end with a 'So,' sentence. The coach checks the last sentence of long turns.

techniques.name: Build from what they already know
techniques.summary: New ideas land when they are built step by step from concepts the audience already has. Starting from the listener's existing model keeps you from losing them.
techniques.how_to_apply: Identify one concept the audience already holds and anchor your explanation to it before adding the new piece.
techniques.drill: Explain a complex part of your strategy to a non-specialist in two minutes, starting from something they already know.

sources.where: TED Talks: building the idea from familiar concepts
Resonate: start where the audience is

techniques.name: Signal the transitions
techniques.summary: Short transition lines ('That's the cost side; now the risk') tell listeners where they are. They make long contributions feel organised and make it harder to be interrupted mid-structure.
techniques.how_to_apply: When moving between parts, say where you've been and where you're going in one short sentence.
techniques.drill: Present a three-part update and record it; check that each part is introduced with a one-line transition.

techniques.name: Know, feel, do: define your intent first
techniques.summary: Before any important communication, decide what you want the listener to know, feel and do afterwards. Without that, people over-explain and drift.
techniques.how_to_apply: Write the three lines before the meeting; open with the 'do' if it is a request, with the 'know' if it is an update.
techniques.drill: Before the next three key meetings, write know/feel/do. The coach checks whether the 'do' was said aloud.

sources.where: Power of Presence: intention and feeling

techniques.name: Cut diffuse hedges from recommendations
techniques.summary: Stacked hedges ('I sort of think maybe') lower credibility and persuasion. In recommendation and decision turns, say what you think.
techniques.how_to_apply: In recommendation turns, delete 'just', 'sort of', 'maybe', 'I guess', 'a bit'. Keep at most one precise qualifier, after the claim.
techniques.drill: The coach lists your top five hedge phrases each week; pick one to drop in recommendation turns for the next week.

techniques.name: Commit, then qualify once
techniques.summary: State your position first, then the single most important uncertainty and how you will handle it. Committed and calibrated beats both diffuse hedging and blanket certainty.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use the pattern: 'I recommend X. The main risk is Y; here's how we'd handle it.' One qualifier, after the commitment.
techniques.drill: Practise five recommendations aloud using the commit-then-qualify pattern; the coach checks order in the transcript.

sources.where: Tenney et al.: calibration trumps confidence

techniques.name: Put a number on your confidence
techniques.summary: People do not dislike uncertain advice when it is expressed precisely (ranges, probabilities, 'more likely than'). Vague 'I'm not sure' is what costs credibility.
techniques.how_to_apply: Replace 'I'm not sure' with a likelihood, range or comparison: '70%', 'between 3 and 5 weeks', 'more likely than not'.
techniques.drill: For a week, every time you would say 'not sure', give a percentage or range instead. The coach counts calibrated phrases.

sources.where: Gaertig & Simmons 2018: uncertain advice not disliked when precise

techniques.name: Say what would change your mind
techniques.summary: Naming the evidence that would change your view shows confidence and openness at once. It reads as conviction held for reasons, not ego.
techniques.how_to_apply: After stating a position on a contested topic, add one line: 'What would change my mind is...'
techniques.drill: In the next two debates, add a 'change my mind' line after your position.

techniques.name: Drop the permission tags
techniques.summary: Tags like 'does that make sense?', 'is that OK?' or 'right?' after a recommendation turn it into a request for approval. Tag questions lower perceived power and credibility.
techniques.how_to_apply: End recommendations with a full stop. If you want input, ask a real question: 'What would you push back on?'
techniques.drill: The coach lists every tag after a recommendation for one week. Replace each with a full stop or a genuine open question.

sources.where: Hosman & Siltanen: tag questions and perceived power

techniques.name: Contribute without apologising
techniques.summary: Opening with 'sorry, can I just...' or 'this might be a silly question' frames your contribution as an imposition and lowers its weight before you start.
techniques.how_to_apply: Start with the content. If you need to break in, use the other person's name and a bridge ('Sam, building on that...').
techniques.drill: For one week, no 'sorry' to open a contribution. The coach counts turn-opening apologies.

techniques.name: Use 'I' for judgements and decisions
techniques.summary: Presence includes owning your view. 'People are saying' or 'it was felt that' hides the judgement; 'I recommend' or 'my view is' owns it. Keep 'we' for shared work.
techniques.how_to_apply: When giving a judgement, use first person singular; when describing team work, use 'we'.
techniques.drill: Review three past recommendations; rewrite each opening line in first person, and use that form next time.

techniques.name: Give a verdict at the decision point
techniques.summary: When the room needs a position, give one: yes, no, or not yet with a date. Executives name decisiveness as a core gravitas trait; dithering at decision points costs more than an imperfect call.
techniques.how_to_apply: When asked for a decision, open with the verdict word, then the reason. If you need more data, say exactly what and by when.
techniques.drill: In the next five decision moments, open with a verdict word. The coach checks first words.

sources.where: 2022 survey: confidence and decisiveness remain top

techniques.name: Do not overclaim
techniques.summary: Confidence attracts trust at first, but confident sources who turn out to be wrong lose more credibility than cautious ones. Certainty should match your evidence.
techniques.how_to_apply: Match your words to your evidence: 'I know' for facts you have checked, 'I expect' for forecasts, 'I suspect' for hunches.
techniques.drill: For one week, tag each claim you make in meetings as know/expect/suspect in your notes afterwards and check your wording matched.

techniques.name: Express confidence you actually have
techniques.summary: Listeners prefer advisors who sound confident, often even when they are overconfident. If you are confident, sound it; under-signalling real confidence leaves influence on the table.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you are sure, say so plainly and once: 'I'm confident about this because...'
techniques.drill: Pick the three topics where you have the strongest evidence; prepare one confident sentence for each and use it when they come up.

techniques.name: Translate British understatement on serious points
techniques.summary: Understatement ('not ideal', 'a bit behind') is normal in UK business but can hide the severity of an issue, especially for international or direct-culture listeners. On serious points, say the plain version.
techniques.how_to_apply: When the issue is serious, state its size plainly, then soften the delivery if needed with tone rather than words.
techniques.drill: Take three understated lines from recent transcripts and rewrite them with the plain severity; use that phrasing in the next international call.

techniques.name: Hold your position under first pushback
techniques.summary: Folding at the first challenge signals that the view was not really held. Restate your position with reasons unless you hear a new fact or argument.
techniques.how_to_apply: When challenged, ask yourself: is this new information? If not, acknowledge and restate. If yes, say so and update openly.
techniques.drill: In a practice debate, hold your view through two challenges without new facts, then update when a new fact is introduced.

techniques.name: Strategic modesty when your expertise is known
techniques.summary: One study found that established experts who expressed some uncertainty were more persuasive (surprise draws attention), but a large 2024 replication did not support this and found certainty helped regardless. Treat as an experiment, not a rule.
techniques.how_to_apply: Where everyone already knows you are the expert, you might try opening with a measured, less-than-certain framing and see how it lands.
techniques.drill: Try it in two expert contexts and compare engagement with two where you open confidently. Report as personal data only.

sources.where: Karmarkar & Tormala 2010; Løhre et al. 2024 replication

techniques.name: A short story with a point
techniques.summary: A brief anecdote with a person, a moment and a point is more persuasive than an abstract claim: listeners get absorbed and notice fewer weak points. Stories are among the charismatic tactics that raise leadership ratings.
techniques.how_to_apply: Tell 30-60 second stories: who, what happened at a specific moment, and the one-line point. Lead into the point you are making, not away from it.
techniques.drill: Build a bank of five 45-second work stories, each tagged with the point it makes. Use one in a meeting each week.

sources.where: Charismatic Leadership Tactics: stories and anecdotes

techniques.name: One fresh image for the core idea
techniques.summary: A metaphor or analogy makes an abstract idea concrete and memorable. It is the charismatic tactic most often adopted by others, which spreads your framing.
techniques.how_to_apply: For each main idea, find one image from everyday life. Use it early and repeat it once.
techniques.drill: Rewrite your current strategic message using one metaphor; test it on two colleagues and keep the one they repeat back.

sources.where: Tur et al. 2022: verbal charisma in TED

techniques.name: Not this, but that
techniques.summary: Contrasts ('not a cost problem, a speed problem') sharpen the point by showing what it is not. They are among the most effective charismatic tactics and give the voice a natural place to stress.
techniques.how_to_apply: Frame your main point as a contrast with the obvious or old view, and stress the contrasting words.
techniques.drill: Turn your next headline into a not-X-but-Y line and deliver it with stress on X and Y.

sources.where: Resonate: contrast between what is and what could be

techniques.name: Lists of three
techniques.summary: Three-part lists feel complete, are easy to remember, and are one of the verbal charismatic tactics. Two feels thin, four feels like a list.
techniques.how_to_apply: Group supporting points, benefits or actions in threes when it is natural; build to the most important.
techniques.drill: In the next presentation, use one deliberate three-part list per main section and check the third item is the strongest.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: rule of three

techniques.name: Ask the question, then answer it
techniques.summary: A rhetorical question creates a gap the audience wants filled; answering it yourself delivers the point with momentum.
techniques.how_to_apply: Pose the question your audience is silently asking, pause briefly, then answer it.
techniques.drill: Put one rhetorical question into your next update at the point where people usually push back.

techniques.name: Reflect the room's sentiment
techniques.summary: Naming what the group is feeling ('I know everyone's tired of re-planning') shows you understand them, which is one of the verbal charismatic tactics and earns permission for what you say next.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before a demanding message, put the group's likely feeling into one sentence, accurately and without exaggeration.
techniques.drill: Before your next team-wide message, write one line naming the group's feeling and test it with a colleague for accuracy.

techniques.name: High bar plus belief they can meet it
techniques.summary: Setting a demanding expectation and in the same breath expressing confidence that people can meet it is a charismatic tactic. Either half alone is weaker.
techniques.how_to_apply: Pair the stretch goal with a specific reason you believe it is achievable.
techniques.drill: Rewrite your next target announcement so it contains both a stretch and one concrete reason for confidence.

sources.where: CLTs: high expectations and confidence they can be met

techniques.name: Moral conviction, sparingly
techniques.summary: Expressing why something is right, not just efficient, is part of charismatic signalling. Overused or used in routine operational talk, it sounds inflated.
techniques.how_to_apply: Reserve values language for decisions that really carry it; say it once, plainly.
techniques.drill: Identify the one decision this month that truly carries a values dimension and prepare one sentence about it.

techniques.name: Contrast what is with what could be
techniques.summary: Persuasive presentations alternate between the current reality and the better future, then end on the new future. The gap creates tension the audience wants resolved.
techniques.how_to_apply: Structure a pitch or vision talk as alternating beats of 'today...' and 'imagine instead...', ending on the future and the call to action.
techniques.drill: Storyboard your next pitch as four what-is/what-could-be beats and an ending; rehearse it aloud once.

sources.where: Resonate: sparkline of what is vs. what could be

techniques.name: Engineer one memorable line
techniques.summary: Plan one moment people will remember and repeat: a crisp phrase, a striking number or a vivid image. Repeat it at the start and end.
techniques.how_to_apply: Craft a short, repeatable line for your main point; say it early, use it again to close.
techniques.drill: For your next presentation, write five candidate lines, test them on a colleague, keep the one they remember an hour later.

techniques.name: Teach them something new
techniques.summary: Audiences pay attention to novelty: an unexpected fact, a counter-intuitive finding or a new way of seeing a familiar problem.
techniques.how_to_apply: Lead with the one thing your audience probably does not know yet and that changes how they see the issue.
techniques.drill: Before your next update, find one fact the audience doesn't know and open with it.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: teach something new

techniques.name: Sensory, specific detail
techniques.summary: A few specific sensory details (what someone said, the time, the place) make a story vivid. Generic summaries do not transport listeners.
techniques.how_to_apply: In stories, include one specific detail: a time, a place, a short paraphrase of what someone said.
techniques.drill: Rewrite one of your stock stories with three specific details and tell it aloud.

techniques.name: Self-deprecate the trivial, never the core
techniques.summary: Light self-deprecation about small things (tech, coffee, handwriting) shows ease and warmth. Self-deprecation about your core competence undermines the very trust the room relies on.
techniques.how_to_apply: Keep self-deprecating humour to non-essential traits, and keep it short.
techniques.drill: Each week the coach lists Tom's self-deprecating lines; check none touched core competence.

sources.where: Bitterly et al. 2017: humour and status

techniques.name: Light humour to signal ease
techniques.summary: Successful humour raises perceived confidence and competence; failed or inappropriate humour signals confidence but lowers perceived competence. Low-risk, situational humour is the safest form.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use gentle humour about the shared situation, mainly early in meetings or after tension resolves; avoid it during someone's serious concern.
techniques.drill: Review a month of laughter events with the coach: which lines landed and in what context; repeat the pattern that worked.

techniques.name: Let them hear why you care
techniques.summary: Audiences respond to speakers who visibly care about their subject. Briefly saying why something matters to you personally adds energy and credibility.
techniques.how_to_apply: In a pitch or big update, include one sentence on why this matters to you, then return to them.
techniques.drill: Write one 'why I care' sentence for your current biggest initiative and use it in the next relevant meeting.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: unleash the master within

techniques.name: Connect, then lead
techniques.summary: People judge warmth (can I trust you?) before competence (can you deliver?). Leading with warmth and then showing strength gets strength accepted rather than resisted.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open conversations with a moment of genuine connection or acknowledgement, then move to substance and direction.
techniques.drill: For a week, open each 1:1 and meeting you lead with one genuine acknowledgement line before the agenda.

sources.where: Fiske, Cuddy & Glick 2007: warmth and competence

techniques.name: 'We' for shared work, 'I' for decisions
techniques.summary: Collective pronouns signal you speak for the group; leaders who win elections use them more. But 'I' remains right for owning decisions and mistakes.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use 'we/us/our' for goals and shared work; keep 'I' for judgements, commitments and apologies.
techniques.drill: The coach shows three 'I/my' sentences about shared work from last week; rewrite them as 'we'.

techniques.name: Name and credit specifics
techniques.summary: Crediting a named colleague for a specific contribution signals security and generosity, a core humble-leadership behaviour. Generic thanks does far less.
techniques.how_to_apply: Once per meeting, credit someone by name for something specific they did or said.
techniques.drill: In every meeting this week, name and credit one specific contribution. The coach counts them.

techniques.name: Label what they seem to feel
techniques.summary: Naming the other person's likely emotion or concern ('it sounds like this has been frustrating') shows you understand and tends to defuse it. It is the core of Voss's tactical empathy.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use 'It sounds like / seems like / looks like...' followed by the emotion or concern, then stop and let them respond.
techniques.drill: In the next three difficult 1:1s, use at least one label and wait silently for the response.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference: labelling, tactical empathy

techniques.name: Single-task attention
techniques.summary: Presence in Cabane's sense is giving full attention to the person in front of you; people sense split attention quickly, even on calls.
techniques.how_to_apply: Close other windows, put the phone away, and keep your attention on what the person is saying rather than on your next point.
techniques.drill: In five 1:1s this week, ask at least one question that uses the other person's exact words. The coach checks.

techniques.name: Second-circle energy
techniques.summary: Rodenburg describes three states: withdrawn (first circle), broadcasting at people (third circle), and connected two-way exchange (second circle). Presence lives in the second, with flexibility to use the others deliberately.
techniques.how_to_apply: Notice when you are withdrawing (looking down, quiet, waiting) or broadcasting (talking at the room, not reading it), and return to focused exchange with specific people.
techniques.drill: After each meeting this week, note which circle you spent most time in; the coach adds talk_share and question data.

sources.where: The Second Circle / Presence: three circles of energy

techniques.name: Open with a question about them
techniques.summary: Asking about the other person's priorities or situation, and following up on the answer, increases how much they like you. People underestimate this effect.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open 1:1s with a genuine question about their world, then ask one follow-up before turning to your agenda.
techniques.drill: Open every 1:1 this week with a question about them plus one follow-up. The coach counts.

sources.where: Huang et al. 2017: question-asking increases liking

techniques.name: Acknowledge the cost to them
techniques.summary: Recognising the burden or constraint your message places on someone ('I know this lands on your team') signals receptiveness and makes the message easier to accept.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before or after a demanding ask, name its specific cost to the listener in one sentence.
techniques.drill: For each request you make this week, add one sentence acknowledging its cost to the person.

sources.where: Yeomans et al. 2020: acknowledgement as receptiveness

techniques.name: Mirror their key words
techniques.summary: Repeating the last few words or the key phrase someone used encourages them to keep talking and signals that you are tracking. Mimicry in negotiation research improved outcomes.
techniques.how_to_apply: When someone says something important, repeat their key two or three words with a slight upward inflection, then wait.
techniques.drill: Use one mirror in each of three 1:1s this week and note whether the other person expanded.

sources.where: Maddux et al. 2008: mimicry in negotiation

techniques.name: Smile in the voice
techniques.summary: Warmth is audible: a slight smile changes the voice's tone, and listeners on calls hear it. It is one of the simplest warmth cues when there are no visual signals.
techniques.how_to_apply: On greetings, thanks and requests, let a genuine smile shape your voice; keep it for moments that warrant it.
techniques.drill: Record a voicemail-style greeting twice, with and without a smile, and listen back.

techniques.name: Small, relevant self-disclosure
techniques.summary: Sharing a small, relevant personal experience or uncertainty makes you more relatable and authentic, which recent executive surveys weight more than they used to.
techniques.how_to_apply: Occasionally share a brief, relevant personal angle (a lesson, a past mistake), then return to the topic.
techniques.drill: Plan one relevant disclosure for your next mentoring 1:1 and keep it under 30 seconds.

techniques.name: Remember and refer back
techniques.summary: Referring back to something personal or professional the other person mentioned before (a project, a family event) shows they matter to you.
techniques.how_to_apply: Note one thing from each 1:1 and open the next one by asking about it.
techniques.drill: Keep a one-line note after each 1:1 for a month and use it in the next one.

sources.where: Charisma Myth: making people feel important

techniques.name: Two follow-ups before a view
techniques.summary: Follow-up questions are the strongest single listening signal and increase liking. Asking two before giving your view also gathers better information.
techniques.how_to_apply: In 1:1s and problem discussions, ask at least two questions that build on what the person just said before you offer an opinion.
techniques.drill: In each 1:1 this week, ask two follow-ups before giving a view. The coach counts them.

techniques.name: Play it back before responding
techniques.summary: Summarising what you heard before responding shows you listened and checks understanding; in disagreement it lowers heat and makes your reply more persuasive.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before your counterpoint, restate the other view in one sentence and check: 'Have I got that right?'
techniques.drill: Before any disagreement this week, restate the other view in one sentence first. The coach counts paraphrases before counterpoints.

sources.where: Yeomans et al. 2020: acknowledging the other view

techniques.name: Talk the right share for the setting
techniques.summary: Command of the room is not airtime. In 1:1s with reports, talking less than half the time is usually right; in groups, fewer, higher-impact contributions carry more weight.
techniques.how_to_apply: Know your target band before you start (1:1 as manager ~30-50%; group participant ~1/N to 1.5/N), and check yourself at the halfway point.
techniques.drill: For two weeks, the coach reports talk_share per setting; pick the setting furthest from its band and adjust.

techniques.name: Finish the sentence, then yield
techniques.summary: When interrupted on an important point, neither fight (louder, faster) nor fold (stop mid-point). Finish the current sentence at the same volume and pace, then hand over or signal you will return.
techniques.how_to_apply: Keep volume and pace steady, complete the sentence, then say 'let me finish this point, then I want your view' if needed.
techniques.drill: With a colleague interrupting at random, practise finishing sentences at baseline volume. The coach checks loudness during overlaps.

sources.where: Hall et al. 2005: status and nonverbal cues

techniques.name: Invite the quiet person by name
techniques.summary: Drawing in someone who has not spoken, with a specific question, shows command of the room and widens the information you get.
techniques.how_to_apply: In each group meeting, name one person who has not spoken and ask a specific, answerable question.
techniques.drill: In every group meeting this week, invite one quiet person by name. The coach checks who spoke after.

techniques.name: Do not interrupt to agree
techniques.summary: Supportive interruptions ('yes, exactly, and also...') still take the floor and can read as dominance or impatience. Let people land their point.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you agree, wait for the end of the sentence, then build: 'Building on that...'
techniques.drill: The coach lists your competitive interruptions for a week; aim to halve them the next week.

techniques.name: Ask, then wait
techniques.summary: After asking a real question, the silence that follows is where the good answer forms. Filling it, rephrasing or answering it yourself kills it.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask your question once, then count silently to five before saying anything else.
techniques.drill: In two meetings, after each open question, count to five silently. The coach measures the gaps.

sources.where: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: listening and pauses

techniques.name: One question at a time
techniques.summary: Stacking several questions in one turn lets the other person pick the easiest and signals nervousness. One clear, open question commands more.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask a single open question ('what', 'how') and stop.
techniques.drill: For a week, the coach flags every stacked question; rewrite two of them as single open questions.

techniques.name: Check in when the signals change
techniques.summary: Presence includes noticing when the room has shifted (confusion, disagreement, low energy) and adjusting out loud rather than ploughing on.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you sense a shift, name it briefly and change approach: shorter, a different example, or a question.
techniques.drill: In your next presentation, plan two checkpoints where you read the room and adjust if needed.

techniques.name: Receive and appreciate while listening
techniques.summary: Small audible signals that you are taking it in ('mm', 'right') keep the speaker going and show presence, especially on calls where nods are invisible.
techniques.how_to_apply: On calls, use brief back-channels at natural pauses; do not take the floor with them.
techniques.drill: On your next three calls, use back-channels deliberately and ask the other person afterwards if you seemed engaged.

techniques.name: Synthesise where the room has got to
techniques.summary: Pulling a scattered discussion together ('So far we agree on A and B; C is open') is a high-presence move: it shows you were tracking everyone and helps the group move.
techniques.how_to_apply: When discussion loops, summarise in one or two sentences what is agreed and what remains open.
techniques.drill: In each group meeting this week, offer one synthesis when the discussion loops.

techniques.name: Listen for the question behind the question
techniques.summary: Many questions carry an unstated concern (a cost question is often about risk or credibility). Answering the real concern shows depth and command.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before answering, ask yourself what the person is really worried about; answer the literal question briefly, then the underlying one.
techniques.drill: After your next Q&A, list each question and the concern behind it; check whether you addressed both.

techniques.name: Command through calm, not volume
techniques.summary: In a noisy or heated room, dropping your volume slightly and slowing down often draws attention better than raising your voice.
techniques.how_to_apply: When the room is loud or scattered, pause, then speak a little quieter and slower to bring people in.
techniques.drill: In the next heated discussion, try one deliberately quieter intervention and note the effect.

techniques.name: Acknowledge, answer, add
techniques.summary: Respond to challenge in three beats: acknowledge the point in one sentence, answer directly (yes, no, a number), add the reason or next step. Receptive replies are rated better and persuade more.
techniques.how_to_apply: Practise the three beats until automatic; keep the acknowledgement genuine and short.
techniques.drill: Have a colleague fire ten tough questions; answer each with acknowledge-answer-add. The coach scores first sentences.

techniques.name: Answer, detail, describe value
techniques.summary: A Q&A structure: give the answer, support it with one specific example, then say why it matters to the person who asked.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use it for questions after presentations and from senior stakeholders; adjust order if a quick example is needed first.
techniques.drill: Prepare five likely questions for your next presentation and draft ADD answers under 30 seconds each.

techniques.name: Neutralise the loaded question
techniques.summary: Paraphrasing a hostile or loaded question into neutral terms before answering buys time, shows you listened, and stops you repeating the hostile framing.
techniques.how_to_apply: Restate the core of the question without its loaded words, then answer the neutral version.
techniques.drill: Write five hostile questions you might face and practise a neutral paraphrase for each.

sources.where: media training: do not repeat the negative

techniques.name: Answer, then bridge
techniques.summary: Bridging moves from the question to your key message ('what matters most here is...'). Done after a genuine answer, it keeps a conversation on track; done instead of an answer, it reads as evasion.
techniques.how_to_apply: Give a short real answer first, then use a bridging phrase to link to your key message.
techniques.drill: In a mock Q&A, answer every question in one sentence before bridging. The coach checks for an answer before each bridge.

techniques.name: Answering a different question (recognise, do not use)
techniques.summary: Speakers can answer a similar but different question fluently, and listeners often fail to notice; detection rises sharply when the question is visible. It works in the moment and damages trust when caught.
techniques.how_to_apply: The coach should flag this in Tom's own replies so he can answer the real question instead. Not to be practised.
techniques.drill: Review three tough questions from recent recordings: did each reply contain the answer type asked for? Rewrite any dodge as a direct answer.

techniques.name: Label the heat
techniques.summary: When a challenger is angry or anxious, naming the emotion calmly ('it sounds like this has caused real problems for your team') often lowers the temperature faster than arguing facts.
techniques.how_to_apply: Label first, pause, then address the substance. Use a calm, slower register.
techniques.drill: Role-play two angry-stakeholder scenarios with a colleague, opening each reply with a label.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference: labelling negatives

techniques.name: Name their objections before they do
techniques.summary: Before a tough message, list the criticisms the other side is likely to have and voice them first. It takes the sting out and often prompts them to soften.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open a hard conversation with two or three of the likely objections, stated fairly and without exaggeration.
techniques.drill: Before the next difficult message, write the three things they'll think, and open with them.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference: accusation audit
Pre-Suasion / Influence: raising a weakness early

techniques.name: Concede the valid point quickly
techniques.summary: Agreeing fast with the part of a challenge that is right builds credibility for the part you dispute. Emphasising agreement is part of conversational receptiveness.
techniques.how_to_apply: Find what is correct in the challenge, agree with it explicitly, then state where you differ.
techniques.drill: In the next three disagreements, start with a genuine concession. The coach counts receptiveness markers.

techniques.name: Disagree with receptive language
techniques.summary: Phrases that acknowledge the other view, state your claim as your view, and frame positively make disagreements more productive and persuasive, and others notice it even when the speaker doesn't.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use 'I see why you'd say that', 'From my view...', 'Where I see it differently is...' instead of 'That's wrong' or 'To be fair...'.
techniques.drill: The coach lists your defensive phrases from last week; replace each with a receptive equivalent in practice.

sources.where: Radical Candor: care personally, challenge directly

techniques.name: "I don't know" plus a plan
techniques.summary: Admitting you don't know, with a specific plan to find out, preserves credibility; bluffing and being found out costs far more.
techniques.how_to_apply: Say 'I don't know' plainly, then what you'll do and by when. Optionally share your best estimate, labelled as such.
techniques.drill: In a practice Q&A, include three questions you can't answer; use the not-knowing pattern each time.

techniques.name: Treat Q&A as conversation, not combat
techniques.summary: Framing tough questions as a dialogue with someone curious, rather than an attack, changes your voice and posture and reduces defensiveness.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before Q&A, remind yourself that questions mean engagement; respond as you would to a curious colleague.
techniques.drill: Before your next Q&A, write one line reframing it as a conversation; compare Q&A stress markers afterwards.

sources.where: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: Q&A as dialogue

techniques.name: Lower and slow under fire
techniques.summary: Under attack, the natural stress response pushes pitch up and pace faster. Deliberately keeping pace slower and pitch settled signals composure and helps you think.
techniques.how_to_apply: When challenged, slow your first sentence and keep pitch at baseline; take a breath before answering.
techniques.drill: Record replies to five challenging questions and compare pitch and rate with baseline; repeat until within your normal range.

sources.where: Cheng et al. 2016: pitch and rank

techniques.name: Dare to be dull: aim for good enough
techniques.summary: When put on the spot, trying to be brilliant creates freeze. Aiming for a clear, adequate answer reduces pressure and usually produces a better one.
techniques.how_to_apply: When called on unexpectedly, give a plain, structured answer; drop the aim of being impressive.
techniques.drill: Ask a colleague to spring three questions on you during the week; answer each plainly in under 30 seconds.

sources.where: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: dare to be dull, treat mistakes as missed takes

techniques.name: Buy time honestly
techniques.summary: Saying you need a moment, or restating the question, gives you a few seconds to structure your answer without sounding caught out.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use a short honest buffer ('Let me think about that for a second') or a paraphrase, then answer with a structure.
techniques.drill: Practise five unexpected questions using a buffer and a two-point structure.

techniques.name: Prepare a message house
techniques.summary: Before a high-stakes meeting or interview, prepare one headline message and three supporting pillars with evidence. Under pressure you return to the house instead of improvising.
techniques.how_to_apply: Write the headline (roof) and three pillars with one proof each on a single card; return to them when answering.
techniques.drill: Build a message house for your next board or investor meeting and rehearse answering five questions from it.

sources.where: media training: key messages and message house

techniques.name: Lead with a weakness before the strengths
techniques.summary: Mentioning a genuine drawback early (and then your strongest points) makes you come across as more honest and makes the strengths more believable.
techniques.how_to_apply: When presenting a proposal, name its main real limitation briefly, then the strengths that outweigh it.
techniques.drill: Rewrite your next proposal opening so it names one real limitation in the first two sentences.

sources.where: Pre-Suasion / Influence: credibility via an early weakness

techniques.name: One idea in fifteen words
techniques.summary: Every talk or contribution should carry one main idea you can state in a single short sentence. If you cannot, the message is not ready.
techniques.how_to_apply: Write the throughline in 15 words or fewer before any important meeting; everything you say should serve it.
techniques.drill: Before your next three key meetings, write your throughline in 15 words; afterwards, ask one attendee what your point was.

techniques.name: Halve it
techniques.summary: Most answers are better at half the length. Senior listeners reward economy; length often reads as uncertainty or lack of preparation.
techniques.how_to_apply: Re-record or rewrite your answer at half the length, keeping the headline and the strongest reason.
techniques.drill: Pick your longest answer from last week's transcript and re-record it at half the length; the coach compares word counts.

techniques.name: Thirty-second answers upward
techniques.summary: With senior stakeholders, aim to answer most questions in about thirty seconds, then offer more detail if wanted. It shows command and respects their time.
techniques.how_to_apply: Answer, give one reason, then stop and offer: 'Want the detail?'
techniques.drill: Practise ten likely senior questions with a timer; aim for 30 seconds each.

sources.where: Simply Said: right level of detail for the audience

techniques.name: Attach the so-what to every fact
techniques.summary: Facts without implications make the listener do the work. Executives want to know what a number means for them.
techniques.how_to_apply: After each fact, add 'which means...' or 'so...' in the listener's terms.
techniques.drill: Review a recent update; add a 'which means' after each number and present the revised version.

sources.where: Get to the Point: 'so what' test

techniques.name: Lead with the ask
techniques.summary: When you need something (a decision, money, help), say so at the start. Burying the ask after context makes listeners wonder what the meeting is for.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open with what you need and by when; then give the reasons.
techniques.drill: For every meeting you request this week, put the ask in the first sentence. The coach checks first-minute asks.

sources.where: Simply Said: what you want them to do

techniques.name: Skip the backstory
techniques.summary: Chronological backstory before the point is the most common cause of long, unclear contributions. Context should come only as needed to support the conclusion.
techniques.how_to_apply: Start with the conclusion; add backstory only if asked or if one fact is essential.
techniques.drill: The coach flags your three longest chronological openings this week; re-record each starting from the conclusion.

techniques.name: Make one number meaningful
techniques.summary: One well-chosen number, put into context (a comparison or a picture), lands better than a slide of figures.
techniques.how_to_apply: Choose the one number that matters and compare it to something familiar.
techniques.drill: For your next update, pick one number and write a comparison for it.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: making statistics meaningful

techniques.name: Three headlines before the meeting
techniques.summary: Writing down the two or three things you most want to say before a meeting means you say them early and crisply rather than discovering them mid-sentence.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before the meeting, write up to three one-sentence headlines; make sure each gets said.
techniques.drill: Before five meetings this week, write three headlines. The coach checks how many were said and when.

techniques.name: Stop when you're done
techniques.summary: Adding 'just one more thing' or repeating a point in different words dilutes the message and signals uncertainty that it landed.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you have made your point, stop. If you have one more genuinely new point, signal it ('one final, separate point').
techniques.drill: The coach flags every repeated point within a turn for a week; aim to cut them by half.

techniques.name: Status, risk, ask
techniques.summary: A three-part update for senior audiences: where we are, the main risk, and what you need. It replaces long progress narratives.
techniques.how_to_apply: Structure updates as one sentence each for status, risk and ask.
techniques.drill: Deliver your next three updates in status-risk-ask form and time them.

techniques.name: Strip jargon and acronyms
techniques.summary: Jargon and internal acronyms make you sound like you are hiding behind language and lose people outside your team. Plain words sound more senior, not less.
techniques.how_to_apply: Replace acronyms and buzzwords with plain words, or define them once.
techniques.drill: The coach lists your top five jargon terms of the week; find a plain replacement for each.

techniques.name: Time-box presentations well under the slot
techniques.summary: Shorter presentations hold attention and leave room for discussion; TED caps talks at 18 minutes for this reason. For internal slots, aim to use about half the time to present.
techniques.how_to_apply: Plan to finish presenting at roughly half the allotted time, leaving the rest for questions and decision.
techniques.drill: Rehearse your next presentation with a timer set to half the slot.

techniques.name: Bad news early, with a plan
techniques.summary: Raising bad news early and plainly, with a recommendation attached, is a mark of gravitas; executives list speaking truth to power among presence traits.
techniques.how_to_apply: Put the bad news in the first sentence or two, state its size plainly, then your recommended response.
techniques.drill: For your next difficult update upward, write the first two sentences in advance: the news and the recommendation.

sources.where: Executive Presence: speaking truth to power

techniques.name: Same voice up as across
techniques.summary: Presence with a board or investors means sounding like you do with peers: same pace, pitch and directness. The usual tell is pitch and pace rising and hedges increasing when speaking up.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before senior meetings, remind yourself to speak as a colleague; compare your recordings across settings.
techniques.drill: The coach produces a side-by-side of your voice and hedge measures in senior vs. peer meetings; pick the biggest gap to close.

sources.where: Cheng et al. 2016: vocal signals and rank

techniques.name: Play high or low on purpose
techniques.summary: Gruenfeld (drawing on theatre) describes 'playing high' (authority: fewer words, direct statements, unhurried delivery) and 'playing low' (approachability: questions, deference, warmth). Effective leaders choose deliberately.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before a meeting, decide which you need: high with a sceptical board under challenge, lower with a junior team you want ideas from.
techniques.drill: For one week, label each meeting 'high' or 'low' in advance; the coach checks the questions-to-statements ratio against your label.

sources.where: Acting with Power: playing high and low

techniques.name: Enter by building on the last speaker
techniques.summary: In fast senior discussions, the cleanest way in is to connect to what was just said, then add your point. It earns the floor without fighting for it.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use the previous speaker's name and point as your bridge, then make your contribution in one or two sentences.
techniques.drill: In three group meetings, make your first contribution within the first ten minutes using a build. The coach checks timing.

techniques.name: Open with substance, not deference
techniques.summary: Openers like 'sorry, if I may, just a quick thought' signal low status before the content arrives. A direct, polite entry carries more weight.
techniques.how_to_apply: Start with the person's name or a short bridge, then the point.
techniques.drill: For one week, the coach flags every deferential opener in upward meetings; replace each with a name-plus-point opener.

sources.where: powerless speech: hedges and polite forms

techniques.name: Disagree upward with respect and reason
techniques.summary: Disagreeing with seniors works best when you acknowledge their view, state yours as your judgement, and give a reason. Receptive disagreement is persuasive without being insubordinate.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use: 'I understand why you'd go that way. My concern is X, because Y. I'd suggest Z.'
techniques.drill: Prepare one respectful disagreement for your next senior meeting using the pattern.

techniques.name: Frame for their agenda
techniques.summary: Senior people listen for what matters to them. Framing your point in terms of their priorities shows strategic awareness and earns attention.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before the meeting, identify the senior person's top concern and link your headline to it.
techniques.drill: Before your next senior meeting, write their top priority and connect your headline to it.

sources.where: Executive Presence (Monarth): reading people and managing perception
Pre-Suasion: what is in focus at the moment of decision

techniques.name: Ask the sharp question
techniques.summary: In senior rooms, a precise, curious question often carries more presence than a statement. Influence earned through expertise and curiosity is respected and liked.
techniques.how_to_apply: Prepare one incisive question that shows you've understood the core issue; ask it calmly.
techniques.drill: For each senior meeting this month, prepare one sharp question.

sources.where: Huang et al. 2017: questions and liking

techniques.name: Spell out the bottom line for direct cultures
techniques.summary: British indirectness can be read as weakness or missed entirely by Dutch, German or many US colleagues. With these audiences, state the conclusion and its severity explicitly.
techniques.how_to_apply: In international meetings, say the bottom line explicitly and avoid understatement on key points.
techniques.drill: Before your next international call, rewrite your key point without understatement.

techniques.name: Drop the over-deference
techniques.summary: Excessive thanks, honorifics or 'if I may' in senior rooms signal that you see yourself as junior. Courtesy is good; deference is a status tell.
techniques.how_to_apply: Thank once, use names rather than titles where culturally appropriate, and drop 'if I may' and 'with respect'.
techniques.drill: The coach counts deferential phrases in your next three senior meetings; cut them by half.

techniques.name: Have the one-minute version ready
techniques.summary: Senior slots get cut. Having a one-minute version of your message ready means you hold your ground when time shrinks instead of rushing a ten-minute version.
techniques.how_to_apply: Prepare a 60-second version of every important presentation; if your time is cut, switch to it calmly.
techniques.drill: For your next presentation, rehearse the one-minute version twice.

techniques.name: Prestige, not dominance
techniques.summary: There are two routes to influence: dominance (interrupting, pressure) and prestige (sharing expertise, generosity). Both work, but only prestige is liked and sustains respect.
techniques.how_to_apply: Influence by teaching and sharing know-how freely; avoid floor-grabbing, sarcasm and pressure tactics.
techniques.drill: The coach tallies dominance and prestige cues across a month; review the balance.

sources.where: Cheng et al. 2013: dominance and prestige
Hall et al. 2005: nonverbal status cues

techniques.name: Keep your pitch level when presenting up
techniques.summary: Status nerves show up in the voice: pitch and rate rise when speaking to seniors. Keeping them near your baseline makes you sound like you belong in the room.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before speaking up, breathe out, find your relaxed pitch, and slow the first sentence slightly.
techniques.drill: Record your next two board or investor sessions; the coach compares pitch and rate with peer-meeting baseline.
